articles.title: Bangladesh: UNICEF chief calls for an end to child marriage
articles.summary: At 14, Bushra faced being married off – until community leaders at a UNICEF-supported child protection hub worked with her father to prevent her from being given away against her will.
articles.content:
Her story was one of many heard by the UN children’s agency Executive Director Catherine Russell who on Tuesday called for urgent investment in Bangladesh’s children following a three-day visit to the country.

Ms. Russell urged action on three fronts: ending child marriage and keeping girls in school, delivering on the Government’s commitment to invest five per cent of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) in both education and health, and protecting quality learning for Rohingya refugee and host-community children.

“Keeping girls in school and providing them with the health, education and protection services they need will deliver a brighter future for them, for their communities, and for Bangladesh,” she said.

Married before 18

In Korail, Dhaka’s largest informal settlement, Ms. Russell heard from children and parents how poverty, disrupted education and limited basic services have impacted their lives.

Adolescent girls shared their ambitions and the pressures that can force them out of school and into marriage.

Nearly half – 47.2 per cent – of women in Bangladesh aged 20 to 24 were married before the age of 18, according to the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025.

Child marriage drives girls out of school, fuels early pregnancy and narrows lifelong opportunities. UNICEF is calling for girls to complete secondary school and for loopholes in national law that permit child marriage to be closed.

Meeting senior officials, including State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam, Ms. Russell welcomed the Government’s commitment to increase spending on education and health, while stressing the importance of turning promises into action.

“Budgets reflect priorities,” she said. “Investing in children’s quality education, health, nutrition and protection is investing in Bangladesh’s future.”

‘They cannot lose their education too’

In Cox’s Bazar, home to one of the largest refugee camps in the world, Ms. Russell met Rohingya children and families and visited a UNICEF-supported learning centre, where students and teachers spoke about the importance of education and vocational skills.

Beyond learning, education protects children from exploitation, trafficking, child marriage and recruitment by armed groups, UNICEF said.

“Rohingya children have lost so much to violence, displacement and uncertainty. They cannot lose their education too,” Ms. Russell said. “The world must invest in them, and in the communities that welcomed them.”

Recognizing Bangladesh’s generosity in hosting the refugees, she appealed to the international community to keep supporting both the Rohingya and their host communities, warning that as humanitarian funding declines, sustained support is critical to protect essential services.

In Cox’s Bazar, UNICEF and partners provide life-saving and essential services to Rohingya refugee children and families.

As humanitarian funding declines sustained international support is critical to protect essential services and ensure that refugee and host-community children are not left behind.

articles.personality_title: UNICEF urges Bangladesh to end child marriage and boost education for girls
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In Bangladesh, many girls marry before they turn 18, which often stops them from continuing school and limits their future opportunities. The country also hosts a large number of Rohingya refugees, including many children who need education and protection.

**What happened** – UNICEF’s head, Catherine Russell, visited Bangladesh for three days. She met with community leaders, government officials, and children, including a girl named Bushra who was saved from child marriage through local support. Ms. Russell called on the government to invest more in education and health, and to protect the rights of both Bangladeshi and Rohingya children.

**Impact** – Nearly half of young women in Bangladesh were married before 18, which harms their education and health. UNICEF’s work helps keep girls in school and stops early marriage. Protecting refugee children’s education also prevents dangers like exploitation and child marriage. The government’s promise to spend more on education and health shows a chance to improve many children’s lives.

**What's next step** – The government needs to turn its promises into real actions by increasing budgets for schools and health services. International donors are also urged to keep supporting both refugees and local communities, so children have access to learning and protection.

**One-sentence takeaway** – UNICEF calls for stronger efforts in Bangladesh to end child marriage and ensure all children, including refugees, can stay safe and learn in school.
articles.personality_title_fr: L'UNICEF appelle le Bangladesh à mettre fin au mariage des enfants et à renforcer l'éducation des filles
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Au Bangladesh, de nombreuses filles se marient avant 18 ans, ce qui les empêche souvent de continuer leurs études et limite leurs chances pour l'avenir. Le pays accueille aussi de nombreux réfugiés Rohingyas, dont beaucoup d'enfants qui ont besoin d'éducation et de protection.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – La directrice de l'UNICEF, Catherine Russell, a visité le Bangladesh pendant trois jours. Elle a rencontré des leaders communautaires, des responsables gouvernementaux et des enfants, dont Bushra, une fille sauvée du mariage forcé grâce au soutien local. Mme Russell a demandé au gouvernement d'investir davantage dans l'éducation et la santé, et de protéger les droits des enfants bangladais et réfugiés.

**Impact** – Près de la moitié des jeunes femmes au Bangladesh se marient avant 18 ans, ce qui nuit à leur éducation et santé. Le travail de l'UNICEF aide à garder les filles à l'école et à empêcher le mariage précoce. Protéger l'éducation des enfants réfugiés évite aussi des dangers comme l'exploitation et le mariage forcé. La promesse du gouvernement d'augmenter les dépenses pour l'éducation et la santé représente une chance d'améliorer la vie de nombreux enfants.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement doit transformer ses promesses en actions concrètes en augmentant les budgets pour les écoles et les services de santé. Les donateurs internationaux sont aussi appelés à continuer de soutenir les réfugiés et les communautés locales, pour que les enfants aient accès à l'apprentissage et à la protection.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L'UNICEF appelle à renforcer les efforts au Bangladesh pour mettre fin au mariage des enfants et garantir que tous les enfants, y compris les réfugiés, puissent apprendre et être protégés à l'école.
articles.personality_title_es: UNICEF insta a Bangladesh a acabar con el matrimonio infantil y mejorar la educación de las niñas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En Bangladesh, muchas niñas se casan antes de los 18 años, lo que a menudo les impide continuar sus estudios y limita sus oportunidades futuras. El país también acoge a un gran número de refugiados rohinyás, incluidos muchos niños que necesitan educación y protección.

**Qué pasó** – La directora de UNICEF, Catherine Russell, visitó Bangladesh durante tres días. Se reunió con líderes comunitarios, funcionarios del gobierno y niños, incluida una niña llamada Bushra que fue protegida de un matrimonio infantil gracias al apoyo local. La señora Russell pidió al gobierno que invierta más en educación y salud, y que proteja los derechos de los niños bangladesíes y refugiados rohinyás.

**Impacto** – Casi la mitad de las mujeres jóvenes en Bangladesh se casaron antes de los 18 años, lo que afecta su educación y salud. El trabajo de UNICEF ayuda a que las niñas permanezcan en la escuela y previene el matrimonio temprano. Proteger la educación de los niños refugiados también evita peligros como la explotación y el matrimonio infantil. La promesa del gobierno de aumentar el gasto en educación y salud representa una oportunidad para mejorar la vida de muchos niños.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno debe convertir sus promesas en acciones reales aumentando los presupuestos para escuelas y servicios de salud. Se insta también a los donantes internacionales a seguir apoyando tanto a los refugiados como a las comunidades locales, para que los niños tengan acceso a la educación y protección.

**Resumen en una frase** – UNICEF pide esfuerzos más fuertes en Bangladesh para acabar con el matrimonio infantil y asegurar que todos los niños, incluidos los refugiados, puedan estar seguros y aprender en la escuela.

articles.title: How a civic tech platform is helping women in Serbia get home safely
articles.summary: “Many incidents of harassment, intimidation, or discomfort in public spaces never become official complaints. Some women do not believe reporting will lead to change.”
articles.content:
This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

For many women and girls in Serbia, safety is not only a question of physical protection. It influences their freedom of movement, their choices, and their ability to participate equally in public life. This issue cannot be viewed separately from the broader social position of women and young people. Reports by the Youth Umbrella Organisation of Serbia (KOMS) show that many young people experience insecurity, declining trust in institutions, and limited opportunities for meaningful participation in decisions that affect their lives. The reports also document concerning cases of pressure, threats, and security risks faced by young activists who publicly advocate for social change.

At the same time, reports of the Commissioner for the Protection of Equality highlight that gender-based discrimination and unequal treatment remain persistent challenges in Serbian society, affecting women and girls in various aspects of their everyday lives. Many incidents of harassment, intimidation, or discomfort in public spaces never become official complaints. Some women do not believe reporting will lead to change. Others fear judgment, social stigma, or consider their experience too minor to be important — but no experience is too small when it concerns the right to dignity, freedom of movement, and equal access to public spaces.

Global Voices conducted an email interview with Varvara Lazarevic, the head of an NGO in Novi Sad, Serbia, to find out what can be done about this universal problem. The NGO, Omladina JAZAS Novi Sad, and their project, SafeSteps, a civic technology platform where women can anonymously share their experiences of insecurity in public spaces, are presented here as an Impact Spotlight for the Serbian edition of the Digital Sparks Program.

Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Varvara Lazarevic (VL): Omladina JAZAS Novi Sad has been working with young people and different marginalized groups for many years, with a focus on improving quality of life through education, information and support. We founded Omladinske novine, a youth media outlet with both print and online editions, and since last year, we have also had our own podcast studio, where we work with young people and teach them about journalism, social media and media production.



Digital Sparks was important to us because it gave us the opportunity to connect areas we have been working on for years — communication, human rights and youth work — with technology. and turn them into a practical tool.



This is how Safe Steps was created. The idea had been developing for years through my professional work, research and work with young people and women. I wanted to explore how technology could become genuinely useful to people and give visibility to experiences that often remain unheard.

GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

VL: For a long time, I had been thinking about experiences that happen every day but rarely become part of any official record. Someone changes the route home, walks faster through a certain part of town, sends a message to say they have arrived safely, or simply starts avoiding a particular place. All of these experiences tell us something about how people actually experience public space.



When we talk about safety, the focus often falls on what individuals should do to protect themselves. I wanted to ask a different question: what can we change in the spaces where people live, work, study and spend their free time?



SafeSteps grew out of that question. It gives people a way to anonymously share their experiences and mark the places where they happened. One experience can point to a problem, while several experiences can reveal a pattern. That can open a conversation with the community and institutions about what could be changed.

GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

VL: The most important thing we did was turn an idea into a functioning platform. SafeSteps is now live, and people can share their experiences and mark places where they experienced violence, harassment, discrimination or felt unsafe.



Privacy was one of our main principles from the beginning. The platform works anonymously, without registration or the need to provide a name, email address or phone number. Locations are shown approximately, so that an experience can be connected to a public space while personal privacy remains protected.



At the same time, we started building communication around the platform through social media and media outreach, explaining how SafeSteps works and encouraging people to share their experiences.



Another important part of the platform is a network of more than 20 support contacts, where people can find information about different forms of assistance.

GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

VL: I think the most important change is that we have created another way for people to make their experiences visible. There are experiences that someone may want to share, but they also need a space where they feel safe and have control over the information they provide.



SafeSteps offers exactly that. A person can share an experience anonymously and, at the same time, contribute to a broader picture of how people experience public space.



For the young people we work with, the project is also a concrete example of how technology can be used for much more than communication and entertainment. It can be a tool for participation and for starting conversations about issues that affect their everyday lives.



We are still at an early stage, so I think it is important to be realistic about long-term impact. For now, we are focused on understanding the experiences being shared and seeing how they can contribute to conversations about possible changes.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed through your participation in the project?

VL: I was already working at the intersection of communication, media, human rights and new technologies before this project. However, SafeSteps made me look at technology much more concretely as part of civic space.



I became especially aware of the role of trust. When you ask people to share sensitive experiences, the way technology is designed becomes just as important as the idea behind it. Privacy, data protection and digital security are not only technical issues. They directly affect whether people feel comfortable participating.



I also learned to think more carefully about the whole journey of information — from the moment a person shares an experience, through the way it is protected and processed, to how it can eventually support communication, research or dialogue with institutions.



For me, this is an important part of digital democracy: creating practical and trustworthy ways for people to participate in the communities they are part of.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

VL: One of the most important things I have learned is that technology itself is not the solution. It becomes meaningful when it responds to a real need and is designed responsibly.



Another important lesson is about privacy. When working with sensitive experiences, data protection has to be considered from the very beginning. People’s trust is built through every part of the platform.



The experience of collaboration that Digital Sparks brought was also very valuable to me. I saw how much knowledge exists among organizations working on similar issues and how much we can learn from one another.



And perhaps the most important lesson is that one voice can start a conversation. Several voices can reveal a pattern. Once a problem becomes visible, there is an opportunity to talk about how it can be addressed.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

articles.personality_title: SafeSteps platform helps women in Serbia share safety concerns anonymously
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In Serbia, many women and girls feel unsafe in public spaces but often do not report their experiences because they fear judgment or think nothing will change. This affects their freedom to move around and participate fully in society.

**What happened** – A group called Omladina JAZAS Novi Sad created SafeSteps, a website where women can anonymously share where and how they felt unsafe. The platform was developed with help from the Digital Sparks program, which supports projects combining technology and social change. SafeSteps protects users’ privacy by not asking for names or contact details and shows approximate locations to protect anonymity.

**Impact** – SafeSteps gives women a safe way to make their experiences visible without fear. By collecting many stories, the platform can highlight patterns of harassment or unsafe areas. This helps communities and local leaders understand problems better and think about how to improve public spaces. It also shows young people how technology can be used to support human rights and participation.

**What's next step** – The organization will keep encouraging people to use SafeSteps and study the shared experiences. They hope this information will start conversations with institutions to create safer public places. They also plan to continue improving the platform and build trust by protecting users’ privacy.

**One-sentence takeaway** – SafeSteps is a new tool in Serbia that helps women safely share experiences of insecurity, aiming to make public spaces safer through community awareness and action.
articles.personality_title_fr: SafeSteps aide les femmes en Serbie à partager anonymement leurs préoccupations de sécurité
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En Serbie, de nombreuses femmes et filles se sentent en insécurité dans les espaces publics, mais ne signalent souvent pas leurs expériences par peur d’être jugées ou de ne pas être entendues. Cela limite leur liberté de mouvement et leur participation à la société.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Un groupe appelé Omladina JAZAS Novi Sad a créé SafeSteps, un site web où les femmes peuvent partager anonymement les endroits et les situations où elles se sont senties en danger. La plateforme a été développée grâce au programme Digital Sparks, qui soutient des projets mêlant technologie et changement social. SafeSteps protège la vie privée des utilisateurs en ne demandant pas leur nom ni leurs coordonnées et montre les lieux de manière approximative.

**Impact** – SafeSteps offre un moyen sûr aux femmes de rendre visibles leurs expériences sans crainte. En regroupant plusieurs témoignages, la plateforme peut révéler des tendances d’harcèlement ou des zones dangereuses. Cela aide les communautés et les autorités à mieux comprendre les problèmes et à réfléchir à des solutions pour améliorer la sécurité. Cela montre aussi aux jeunes comment la technologie peut soutenir les droits humains.

**Prochaine étape** – L’organisation continuera d’encourager l’utilisation de SafeSteps et d’analyser les expériences partagées. Elle espère que ces informations lanceront des discussions avec les institutions pour rendre les espaces publics plus sûrs. Elle prévoit aussi d’améliorer la plateforme et de renforcer la confiance en protégeant la vie privée.

**Résumé en une phrase** – SafeSteps est un nouvel outil en Serbie qui aide les femmes à partager en toute sécurité leurs expériences d’insécurité, dans le but de rendre les espaces publics plus sûrs par la prise de conscience et l’action collective.
articles.personality_title_es: SafeSteps ayuda a mujeres en Serbia a compartir anónimamente sus preocupaciones de seguridad
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En Serbia, muchas mujeres y niñas no se sienten seguras en los espacios públicos, pero a menudo no denuncian sus experiencias por miedo a ser juzgadas o a que no sirva de nada. Esto limita su libertad de movimiento y participación en la sociedad.

**Qué pasó** – Un grupo llamado Omladina JAZAS Novi Sad creó SafeSteps, una plataforma donde las mujeres pueden compartir de forma anónima los lugares y situaciones donde se sintieron inseguras. La plataforma se desarrolló con ayuda del programa Digital Sparks, que apoya proyectos que combinan tecnología y cambio social. SafeSteps protege la privacidad de las usuarias al no pedir nombres ni datos de contacto y muestra ubicaciones aproximadas para proteger el anonimato.

**Impacto** – SafeSteps ofrece una forma segura para que las mujeres hagan visibles sus experiencias sin miedo. Al reunir muchas historias, la plataforma puede mostrar patrones de acoso o áreas inseguras. Esto ayuda a las comunidades y a las autoridades a entender mejor los problemas y pensar en cómo mejorar los espacios públicos. También muestra a los jóvenes cómo usar la tecnología para apoyar los derechos humanos.

**Próximo paso** – La organización seguirá animando a la gente a usar SafeSteps y estudiará las experiencias compartidas. Esperan que esta información inicie conversaciones con las instituciones para crear espacios públicos más seguros. También planean seguir mejorando la plataforma y construir confianza protegiendo la privacidad.

**Conclusión en una frase** – SafeSteps es una nueva herramienta en Serbia que ayuda a las mujeres a compartir de forma segura sus experiencias de inseguridad, con el objetivo de hacer los espacios públicos más seguros mediante la conciencia y la acción comunitaria.
